UOB sells 36 of 38 Marina Collection units within two hours
article:
UOB has sold 36 of the 38 Marina Collection units it put up for sale in under two hours, says Dominic Lee, head of luxury and investment sales at PropNex, the sole marketing agent. Based on listed prices, the units sold for about $103.5 million in total, at an average of $1,342 psf.

Marina Collection is a 124-unit condominium on Cove Drive in Sentosa Cove , next to ONE°15 Marina, and was completed in 2011. It sits on a 99-year lease that started in 2007, with about 79 years remaining.

Bookings opened at 10am on Nov 14, and by 11.40am only two units were left. The two units are still available on a first-come, first-served basis, says Lee.

More than 400 groups viewed the units during previews from Nov 6 to 13. A total of 65 cheques were collected as expressions of interest, which means the sale was 1.7 times subscribed. Balloting was held for 12 units that drew multiple bids.

Of the 36 buyers, 23 were Singaporeans, and seven were Permanent Residents (PRs) from countries ranging from China and India to Guatemala and Turkey. The other six were foreigners: five Americans and one Norwegian, says Lee. Under Singapore’s free trade agreements with the US and Norway, these buyers pay stamp duty at the same rates as Singapore citizens, which means no additional buyer’s stamp duty (ABSD) on a first home, rather than the 60% ABSD most foreigners pay.

Most buyers were owner-occupiers, with 31 units purchased for their own use, he adds. “Buyers loved the marina-facing units, as well as the convenience of being close to three supermarkets." They are Cold Storage and Jasons The Gourmet Grocer at Quayside Isle , and Little Farms at Sentosa Arrival Plaza.

Prices for the units sold ranged from $2.588 million ($1,381 psf) for a 1,873 sq ft three-bedroom unit on the second level, to $3.11 million ($1,301 psf) for a 2,390 sq ft four-bedroom unit with a private enclosed space (PES) on the first level. On a psf basis, prices ranged from $1,269 psf for a first-level four-bedroom unit with PES, to $1,407 psf for a second-level three-bedroom unit.

The two remaining units are both on the first level, include PES, and are tenanted until 3Q2027. One is a 2,099 sq ft three-bedroom unit asking $2.786 million ($1,327 psf). The other is a 2,390 sq ft four-bedroom unit listed at $3.064 million ($1,282 psf).

The sale follows the conclusion of UOB’s long-running lawsuit against the developer, Lippo Marina Collection, which the court found liable for conspiring with buyers to inflate the prices of the same 38 units, sold between 2011 and 2013, through undisclosed “furniture rebates”.

UOB had disbursed about $182 million in housing loans for the units, and all 38 buyers later defaulted. In August, the Appellate Division raised the bank’s damages award from $ 17.7 million to $ 76.1 million, and on Oct 21 corrected it to about $82.4 million to include interest that had been left out.

title: Shanghai giant Jin Jiang Hotels accelerates Southeast Asia expansion; HK's Portier Hotels rolls out new brand in Bali
article:
Asia Pacific’s hospitality sector is seeing sustained momentum with more hotels debuting.

Chinese hospitality behemoth Shanghai Jin Jiang International Hotels, for one, is picking up the pace in its expansion across Southeast Asia.

Separately, Hong Kong boutique player Portier Hotels has also launched a fresh collection of lifestyle hotels, The Arc House, starting with a property in Indonesia.

Jin Jiang Hotels is bringing six brands from China to the Southeast Asian market: Ginco Hotel, Renjoy Hotel, Metropole Jinjiang Hotels, Jinjiang Inn, Lavande, and 7 Days Premium.

These brands cover all segments, from economy to high-end products, to adapt to the diverse markets in the region.

In a Nov 12 press release, the Shanghai-listed global hotel group said the construction and rollout of its Southeast Asia projects are “advancing steadily”, and it is growing its regional footprint amid the tourism boom.

It most recently opened the 7 Days Premium Hotel in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, in July 2026. Next in the line-up is the Jinjiang Metropolo Hotels Luang Prabang in Laos, with its grand opening slated for Nov 16.

And in the first half of 2027, the 7 Days Premium Hotel in Jakarta, Indonesia, along with the Renjoy property and a second 7 Days project in Malaysia, will open successively.

Juvena He, general manager of overseas business, Jin Jiang Hotels China Region, pointed to the group’s “belief in Southeast Asia’s boundless potential” and long-term commitment to the region.

To date, Jin Jiang Hotels has three regional offices across Malaysia, Indonesia and Vietnam, with local employees accounting for more than 80% of its workforce.

These offices will work closely with Louvre Hotels Group, a subsidiary of Jin Jiang Hotels, to jointly deepen their footprint in Southeast Asia. Louvre Hotels Group manages over 1,750 properties in 70 countries, through brands such as Première Classe, Hosho, Kyriad, Campanile, Tulip Hotels & Residences, and Sarovar.

Jin Jiang Hotels ranks as the second-largest hotel group in the world by property count and the largest in Asia by room count. As at end-2025, it had invested in or managed more than 14,900 hotels with over 1.51 million rooms in more than a hundred countries.

New boutique lifestyle hotel brand, The Arc House

Meanwhile, Hong Kong-headquartered full-service boutique hospitality group Portier Hotels has introduced The Arc House — a collection of design-forward boutique lifestyle hotels.

The first property under the brand is the newly opened The Arc House Canggu on the southern coast of Bali, Indonesia.

Located near Batu Bolong Beach, the hotel in the Canggu resort village sits within a mix of contemporary dining, independent retail, wellness and nightlife options.

It has 19 suite villas with private pools, alongside an Indo-Japanese restaurant Mykaza, a rooftop infinity pool and wellness programming.

The collection will next expand to Hong Kong later this year with 24 rooms, followed by Melbourne, Australia, in early 2027 with 43 rooms.

In Hong Kong, the property will open at 148 Wellington Street, placing guests close to Central’s art, heritage, dining and city rhythms. This will also feature a lounge, rooftop terrace, gym and a Cantonese restaurant named One Forty Eight Wellington.

The Arc House aims to cater to travellers who want to feel closer to the character of a destination, according to a press release in early November 2026.

Each hotel under The Arc House brand will be shaped by its setting. Edward McKenna, co-founder of Portier Hotels, highlighted that Asia Pacific is a region of “very different travel cultures”, and increasingly guests expect hotels to reflect that richness.

“They look for design, service and food that bring them closer to a place, rather than offering the same experience in every destination,” he added.

In June, EdgeProp Singapore reported that lifestyle hotels — design-led properties that trade standardised comfort for local character, experiential programming and social spaces — are getting more popular in the region amid rising demand from Gen Z and a growing pool of conversion-ready assets .

Real estate consultancy CBRE had said then that lifestyle hotels are among the fastest-growing segments in the global hospitality industry, though such brands are still underpenetrated within Asia Pacific.

In terms of its design language, The Arc House features minimalist interiors and arches. In Canggu, the hotel also showcases locally sourced and commissioned artwork.

Portier Hotels was founded in 2023 and its offerings span hospitality development, operations and management, with properties in Asia Pacific. Besides The Arc House, the group’s portfolio has another brand known as je ne sais quoi.

title: Weaker 2H2026 for CDL as asset sales delayed; offices, malls stay strong
article:
City Developments (CDL) expects its financial performance for 2H2026 to be "significantly weaker" y-o-y, mainly due to the absence of divestment gains. In 2H2025, it booked a $473.1 million gain from the sale of its 50.1% stake in South Beach Consortium to joint venture partner IOI Properties Group .

Capital recycling deals CDL had planned for the rest of FY2026 are now expected to be completed in FY2027, due to "prevailing market conditions with persistent inflationary pressures and elevated interest rates".

Two other factors add to the drag. The Korean won's appreciation against the Singapore dollar since July has resulted in significant foreign exchange losses at CDL's Korean subsidiary, which holds an SGD-denominated intercompany loan receivable.

CDL is also revaluing its property portfolio, which may lead to impairment losses.

The firm’s 3Q2026 operational update was released after market close on Nov 11, when its shares ended the day at $7.12. In early trading the next day, they fell as much as 10.1% to a one-year low of $6.40, before paring losses. By Friday, Nov 13, the shares had closed at $6.64, down 6.7% over the two trading days.

Despite the weaker outlook, its operating assets are holding up. Its offices and luxury retail continue to outperform the wider market, and its Singapore hotels are busier, though rising costs are squeezing margins.

Offices, malls outperform market

CDL's Singapore office portfolio was 97.4% committed as at Sept 30, against an islandwide occupancy rate of 90.0%, based on URA data for 3Q2026. Republic Plaza was 98.0% committed and City House 96.8%. The portfolio has recorded positive rental reversions for three consecutive quarters this year.

The group's two Grade A office developments, Newport Tower and Union Square Central, are on track for completion in 2027 and 2028, respectively. CDL says both are drawing leasing interest from cybersecurity, fintech, financial and professional services firms. It expects tighter Grade A office supply over the next few years to support leasing.

The group's Singapore retail portfolio was 97.1% committed, compared with URA's islandwide rate of 93.5% for 3Q2026. City Square Mall was 97.3% committed, while Palais Renaissance on Orchard Road reached full occupancy, up from 98.6% as at June 30.

Tenant sales at Palais Renaissance rose 71.3% y-o-y, which CDL attributes to stronger spending among its luxury-fashion tenants.

Busier hotels, asset enhancements

For 9M2026, revenue per available room (RevPAR) at CDL's Singapore hotels rose 3.0% y-o-y to $163.3, as occupancy rose 2.7 percentage points to 81.2%. Average room rates (ARR) were broadly flat. CDL says the February Singapore Airshow boosted event-led international visitation.

Yet the Singapore hotels' gross operating profit (GOP) margin fell 2.5 percentage points to 36.4%, as operating costs outpaced revenue.

Two of its Singapore hotels are being refurbished. The 415-room M Hotel Singapore began a phased renovation of its guestrooms and public areas in May, with completion scheduled for 3Q2027.

At the 311-room Copthorne King's Hotel, the tender for refurbishing 169 rooms and public areas in the main wing has been completed. Major works are expected to run from 1Q2027 to 4Q2027.

The refurbishments extend beyond Singapore. In London, a major AEI at the 222-room Millennium Hotel London Knightsbridge is scheduled to start in 4Q2026.

The 833-room Copthorne Tara Hotel London Kensington began the first of three phases of room renovation in October, with the full programme due to be completed by 2Q2029.

In New York, the 124-room Millennium Premier Hotel New York Times Square reopened on June 1 after renovating its guestrooms and public areas. Renovation works at the adjacent 626-room Millennium Hotel Broadway Times Square is due to finish by 4Q2026 for its restaurant and public areas, and by 2H2028 for its rooms.

CDL is also adding a new hotel in the US. The 263-room M Social Hotel Sunnyvale in California is under construction and is expected to open in December 2026.

For 9M2026, group-wide hotel RevPAR rose 6.4% to $175.2, driven by a 2.3 percentage-point rise in occupancy to 75.2% and a 3.1% increase in ARR.

CDL expects RevPAR growth to continue through the rest of 2026, citing event-led demand from the Formula 1 Singapore Grand Prix in October, London's World Travel Market in November and BTS's four-night Singapore concert series in December.

Living sector: some stabilised, some still leasing up

CDL's living sector portfolio spans private rented sector (PRS) housing in Japan, the UK and Australia, and purpose-built student accommodation (PBSA) in the UK.

In Japan, its PRS portfolio of 40 assets and 2,246 units maintained occupancy above 95%. CDL says sustained wage growth and constrained new supply continue to support rental growth.

In the UK, The Junction in Leeds (665 units) was 94% occupied.

Newer assets are still filling up. The Octagon in Birmingham (370 units), which began operations in August 2025, was 56% occupied. The Archive in Melbourne, CDL's first operational PRS asset in Australia, was 65% occupied, with stabilisation expected in 2027.

Its UK PBSA portfolio of six properties and 2,368 beds was 83% occupied as at Sept 30 for the 2026/2027 academic year.

More assets are coming on stream. The YardHouse in London (209 units) reached practical completion in October, and leasing has begun. The Joinery in Manchester (261 units) is expected to complete in 1Q2027.

Gearing at 75%

CDL's net gearing, after factoring in the fair value of investment properties, stood at 75% as at Sept 30.

The group attributes this mainly to capital deployed for the Tanjong Rhu Road and Peck Hay Road government land sales (GLS) sites it won in 1H2026.

In February, a 90:10 joint venture between CDL and Woh Hup won the 131,743 sq ft Tanjong Rhu Road site with a $709.3 million bid, or $1,455 psf per plot ratio (psf ppr). It is slated for a 520-unit, 99-year leasehold condo across three 26-storey blocks with waterfront views. In June, CDL and Hong Realty, a member of Hong Leong Group, won the Peck Hay Road site with a $542.4 million bid ($1,865 psf ppr). The prime District 9 site can be developed into a 39-storey residential tower with 380 units.

Interest cover was 2.7 times. CDL had cash reserves of $2.1 billion, and $4.8 billion in cash and available committed credit facilities.

CDL says it remains committed to GET+, the three-year roadmap for FY2027 to FY2029 it unveiled on Sept 28 following its strategic review. The plan targets $6 billion in divestments, a reduction of about $3 billion in net borrowings and net gearing of about 55% by FY2029.

The group also aims to grow total assets under management across its listed and private platforms to $10 billion. One route it has outlined is seeding suitable assets into managed vehicles.

title: Top Stock Market Highlights of the Week: Nvidia, SGX, US Treasury Yields and Singapore’s Pension Ranking
article:
Welcome to this week’s edition of top stock market highlights.
A chipmaker that was the world’s most valuable company just weeks ago lost its long-time leader this week, and its shares tumbled.
Closer to home, market volatility lifted the local bourse’s derivatives trading volume to a six-month high in October.
Meanwhile, US bond yields climbed back above 5% as investors braced for more interest rate hikes.
And in a bright spot for Singapore, a global pension index ranked the country’s retirement system the best in Asia.
Nvidia’s CEO resigns as scandal deepens
Nvidia
(NASDAQ: NVDA) announced on 12 November 2026 that co-founder and
CEO Jensen Huang
had resigned following reports of two affairs.
Scrutiny began after Huang admitted to a relationship with a former executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed International.
US authorities suspect her of spying for China, a claim Beijing has denied.
A later report said Huang had also had a relationship with a senior Nvidia executive who reported to him.
Chief financial officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent successor.
Board member Harvey Jones has been appointed Nvidia’s first-ever chair.
Huang, who owns about 3.6% of the company, will also leave the board.
The shares fell as much as 14% at the open, pushing Nvidia’s market capitalisation below US$4 trillion for the first time since 2025.
The stock is now roughly 35% below its early-October record, and at least seven Wall Street firms have downgraded it over the past week.
Investors will look to Nvidia’s 3QFY2027 results, due on 17 November 2026, for clarity.
Market volatility lifts SGX’s trading volumes
Singapore Exchange
(SGX: S68) reported on 12 November 2026 that its derivatives daily average volume climbed to a six-month high in October, as volatile markets drove demand for hedging.
Daily average derivatives volume rose 8% year on year and 17% month on month to 1.6 million contracts. FTSE China A50 Index Futures recorded a 24-month high in daily average volume.
Open interest (the value of contracts still outstanding) in GIFT Nifty 50 contracts topped US$20 billion.
Securities market turnover also rose, climbing 32% year on year to S$44.8 billion.
Daily average value reached S$2 billion, driven by trading in index stocks and REITs.
The pick-up came as Singapore shares weakened in October.
The
Straits Times Index
(SGX: ^STI) fell about 5% to 5,376.74, while the FTSE ST Technology Index dropped 17%.
Even so, the STI ended the month 21% higher than a year earlier.
US bond yields climb as bets on rate hikes grow
US Treasury yields rose sharply on 12 November 2026, with the benchmark 10-year yield climbing back above 5% to 5.068%.
The two-year yield, which is more sensitive to Federal Reserve policy, jumped more than 11 basis points (0.11 percentage point) to 4.843%.
Hotter-than-expected consumer price index (CPI) data earlier in the week strengthened expectations of further rate hikes.
Traders are now fully pricing in a hike in December, and
Goldman Sachs
(NYSE: GS) added another quarter-point hike in March 2027 to its forecast.
Oil added to
inflation
worries after President Donald Trump said the US does not need a deal with Iran.
That raised concerns the war in the Middle East could drag on, and Brent crude rose about 1% to US$93.60 a barrel.
Higher rates are already weighing on rate-sensitive sectors.
US existing home sales fell to their lowest level in more than 16 years in October.
For Singapore investors, rising rates could mean higher borrowing costs for REITs.
The impact on local banks is more mixed, as the 3Q2026 results for
DBS Group Holdings Ltd
(SGX: D05),
Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation Limited
(SGX: O39) and
United Overseas Bank Limited
(SGX: U11
)
showed.
Singapore’s retirement system ranks first in Asia
Singapore’s
retirement
system ranked fourth in the world and first in Asia in the Marsh CFA Institute Global Pension Index 2026, released on 20 October 2026.
Singapore scored 82.0 out of 100, earning an A grade alongside just five other systems.
The Netherlands topped the index with 85.8, followed by Denmark (84.1) and Iceland (84.0). Israel and Australia completed the A-grade group.
The index assessed 55 retirement income systems on three measures:
Adequacy (40% weighting)
Sustainability (35%)
Integrity (25%)
It measures the overall strength of each system rather than comparing individual pension payouts.
Singapore finished well ahead of its regional peers.
Hong Kong ranked 17th, Malaysia 35th and Japan 39th, while Thailand, Indonesia and the Philippines were all in the bottom 10.
The US placed 33rd.
A strong national system does not guarantee every individual a comfortable retirement, however. Depending on their goals, investors may still need their own savings and investments.

title: The oil market is brimming with crude despite tanker attacks
article:
(Nov 14): More than eight months into the Iran war, smoke continues to billow from oil tankers as Tehran presses ahead with repeated attacks near the Strait of Hormuz.

And yet there’s more than enough crude on the global market.

Saudi Arabia, the de facto leader of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (Opec), said it pumped 10.5 million barrels a day in October, a level reached only once since 2022. Iraq and Kuwait also reported big increases, while the United Arab Emirates is now free of Opec quotas, allowing it to pump as much as it wants. Gulf shipments nudged lower this week, but remain healthy despite a slew of attacks, according to TankerTrackers.com Inc.

The ample supply has added to pressure on oil prices. Futures at one point this week were down almost 25% for the month, easing inflation concerns and offering respite for the global economy. Prices for physical cargoes have also plummeted, as producers compete for customers and exorbitant shipping costs begin to thaw.

The recovery is still precarious. Attacks have killed at least one seafarer this month and spilled oil is washing ashore on the region’s beaches. With shipping under constant threat and Iranian media claiming attacks on navigational equipment near Hormuz, oil flows are erratic and could slow at any moment.

See also: Oil-hungry Asia turns back to Mideast in earnest as flows expand

But Emirati officials at a recent conference in Abu Dhabi were keen to stress the resilience of the industry. That ability to keep crude flowing, mirrored across the Gulf, has helped bring Middle East shipments back towards pre-war levels and pushed Brent crude prices below US$90 a barrel at one point this week.

“For us national shipping companies, there is no choice,” Khalid Alhammad, president of ship management for Saudi vessel owner Bahri, said at a conference in Dubai. “We still have to go through the Strait of Hormuz. We have to keep moving the energy.”

It’s a remarkable turnaround from some of the worst fears at the outset of the war. Before the conflict, about a fifth of the world’s oil flowed through Hormuz, and analysts warned that a closure could send crude prices above US$200 a barrel.

See also: BP in talks to sell stake in Brazil oil discovery to Petrobras — Bloomberg

Last week at Adipec, the Middle East’s biggest oil conference, senior executives agreed that crude markets look well supplied heading into 2027, with further price declines potentially easing the fight against inflation, though efforts to rebuild stockpiles depleted during the war could limit how far they fall.

The recovery reached a milestone on Friday, when the International Energy Agency (IEA) said oil supply was outpacing demand for the first time since the war began. Rising production beyond the Gulf has helped cushion global markets, with weekly US crude output topping 14 million barrels a day for the first time and the latest figures from Brazil and Guyana all at records.

The IEA said the shift, alongside a plunge in physical crude prices, suggested the market was “showing tentative signs of rebalancing.”

Pockets of tightness persist. Fuel prices remain far higher than crude, with European diesel trading at about US$170 a barrel, for example. Shipping costs are also still historically elevated. Transporting crude from the US to Asia adds roughly 20% to the price of American oil, more than double the premium a year ago.

Yet even those strains have eased. Freight markets remain elevated, but are well below the extremes seen a month ago. US retail gasoline prices have also fallen below US$4 a gallon for the first time since July, according to the American Automobile Association.

“The return of supply from the Gulf has depressed prices, coupled with the deflation of the freight bubble,” said Sasha Foss, an analyst at Marex Group’s CSC Commodities. “The market is less stressed than it was, but October was the biggest month for vessel incidents in Hormuz, so there are still risks.”

The rebalancing has come at a cost. Vitol Group, the world’s top independent oil trader, said recently that the Iran war has cut global oil consumption by about three million barrels a day, an assessment echoed by other major traders. The market, in other words, is finding its footing partly because the war has sharply curtailed demand across fuels and regions.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

China’s crude imports fell about 15% from a year earlier to 9.9 million barrels a day in October. European nations have reported double-digit declines in diesel demand, while US gasoline consumption was marginally lower than a year earlier during the peak summer driving season.

The supply recovery began in earnest over the summer and has gathered pace since then. It shows up in a steady uptick in ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman, as traders unload cargoes onto new ships just outside Hormuz as part of a burgeoning shuttle trade.

It has left traders with plenty of cargoes to sell. This week, Abu Dhabi National Oil Co slashed the price of its flagship crude grade to attract buyers. Saudi Arabia also cut its key oil prices, though the kingdom is selling fewer barrels under long-term contracts than before the war, making its pricing harder to track. Instead, it has increasingly turned to ad hoc sales.

The cuts underscore just how much oil is leaving the Gulf, even as tankers remain under attack.

“The workarounds and the shuttle system have managed to keep these prices from going sky-high,” said John Kilduff, partner at Again Capital. “There’s a question of durability. We’ve gone through a period where the Iranians didn’t cause much havoc in the Strait. But lately, that’s ramped up again, and there’s a concern that this could go off the rails.”

title: Microsoft says services fully restored after outage roiled world
article:
(Nov 14): Microsoft Corp said access has been fully restored to its flagship software, ending an outage that paralysed government offices, traders and businesses around the world.

“All products are operational,” according to a service health status update on its website. A “backlog of email messages has been processed, thus this issue is remediated”, it said of its Microsoft 365 services.

That included Outlook, Teams and the Copilot artificial intelligence tool, whose users experienced missed meeting invitations and unresponsive web pages on Friday. Previous disruptions have rarely lasted more than several hours.

The outage cascaded around the world, with people in more than 70 countries reporting problems, according to Downdetector, which recorded hundreds of thousands of complaints.

Office and government workers from Tokyo to London and New York struggled to adapt, often reaching for analogue 20th-century tools like the telephone and, yes, paper. Corporate workers around the US celebrated the Outlook outage as an “adult snow day”. Google Workspace workers, meanwhile, looked on with envy as their Outlook counterparts kicked up their feet.

But their bosses were already counting the costs. Some companies, including Swiss luxury group Richemont and US-based truck and bus manufacturer Workhorse Group Inc, were forced to delay reporting their financial results. Critical services including police departments and hospitals were affected, with the UK’s National Health Service rescheduling some procedures, according to people familiar with the matter.

See also: Billionaire KoGuan vows to stop buying Nvidia after Huang exit

The failure and the time it took to find a fix was a black eye for Microsoft, whose Windows operating system and productivity apps remain critical infrastructure in the age of artificial intelligence. The company’s M365 software bundle has more than 450 million commercial users. Once again, critics highlighted the risks of entrusting so much power to one provider — even as many people understood that unshackling themselves from Microsoft’s ubiquitous products was unlikely anytime soon. Investors largely shrugged off the incident, with Microsoft shares little changed.

“We do not expect the incident to meaningfully change Microsoft’s competitive position in the near term, given the high cost and complexity of replacing deeply embedded productivity workflows,” William Blair & Co analyst Jason Ader wrote in a note. “Longer term, however, it could make some customers more receptive to alternatives, particularly Google Workspace and emerging productivity offerings from Anthropic unveiled earlier this week.”

The error was introduced during a network capacity upgrade, a spokesperson said. The company’s response, detailed in hourly updates to the company’s status page, described some false starts as Microsoft struggled to pin down the issue.

See also: Microsoft races to fix Outlook in one of its longest outages

More than 1,000 engineers and other employees gathered on video calls led by cloud chief Scott Guthrie and Charles Lamanna, who oversees the M365 bundle and other workplace applications. Sessions ran late Thursday and spilled into Friday morning.

Exchange, the digital backbone powering email and calendars in the M365 bundle, would start up on a server and quickly consume its available resources, leading it to become unresponsive. Engineers investigated whether the application was mistakenly firing traffic at databases rather than local memory, according to a person familiar with the matter. Some suspected a misconfiguration in Microsoft’s Azure cloud network could be at fault.

Publicly, Microsoft said it would provide more detail after the disruption was over, adding that there was no evidence of malicious activity. It was also unrelated to AI or agents, a spokesperson said.

“We know our customers rely on our services to get important work done every day, and regret the impact these outages had on those who depend on us,” Lamanna said in an emailed statement. “Our teams are reviewing what happened and how we can prevent similar issues going forward.”

The first signs that Microsoft was experiencing issues came at about 1pm on Thursday on the US East Coast. Reports began spiking on Downdetector, and disgruntled customers took to social media to gripe and say, essentially, “Here we go again.” Many recalled previous outages, including a 15-hour disruption at Amazon Web Services last year that hit hundreds of websites. And few have forgotten the mother of all outages in 2024, when a faulty software update from cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike Holdings Inc grounded flights and crashed systems around the world, causing billions of dollars in damages.

The latest incident wasn’t so far-reaching, but impactful all the same. PVH Corp, the apparel conglomerate that owns the Calvin Klein and Tommy Hilfiger brands, announced Thursday that it would cut about 4% of its global workforce. But some of the difficult conversations, scheduled to start in Asia on Friday morning, didn’t take place because of the outages, leaving employees uncertain of their future, according to a person familiar with the matters, who requested anonymity to describe private matter. PVH didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

In Arapahoe County, Colorado, which includes some Denver suburbs, the sheriff’s office couldn’t process online bond payments to release detainees from jail because of missing email traffic. People were asked to post bond in person at the jail instead. In Japan, government ministries resorted to pinning up paper notices to inform journalists about daily schedules.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

Lauryn Taylor, an ad sales associate at a US media company, said the outage began around noon on Thursday and continued until she left the office at about 5pm. For her, it was a welcome reprieve from the steady stream of emails that typically distracts her from more in-depth work. Because much of her job doesn’t depend on email, she was able to keep working.

“It was kind of nice to have that focused period,” she said.

Some colleagues whose jobs consist almost entirely of email, meanwhile, left the office to take a yoga class.

The outage disrupted more than just office work. Taylor’s mother ran into trouble Thursday while trying to order wings from Wingstop. Uber Eats asked her to verify her email address, but the message never arrived in her Hotmail inbox.

“She was like, ‘What is going on?’” Taylor said. “She thought she had broken her Outlook somehow or something.”

title: UK's Burnham tries to hush down his own talk of rejoining EU
article:
(Nov 14): Six weeks ago UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham suggested Britain “could go all the way” and rejoin the European Union (EU). This week, he downplayed his own idea: “No one’s talking about rejoining.”

The prime minister heads into a UK-EU summit in Brussels on Nov 20 trying to slow down a conversation he started about the country’s long-term relationship with Europe.

Burnham has been privately making clear to Labour colleagues that he’s not in a rush to decide what he wants his long-term EU policy to be, according to government officials familiar with the matter. Number 10 Downing Street has not even begun discussing which outcome it might favor, according to one. The prime minister is open-minded and keen not to put his thumb on the scale by backing a particular option before much wider consultation with his party, businesses, the public and the EU, they added.

Another official said Burnham’s aides want to tap the brakes on a conversation that’s at risk of getting out of control. In a sign of their caution, Number 10 is undecided on whether to go ahead with a planned speech by Burnham after the summit in which he had intended to set out different options for the future relationship, a third official said. They all spoke on condition of anonymity discussing internal policy deliberations.

Reigniting a debate about Britain’s place in Europe — a decade on from the 2016 referendum — was a decision of Burnham’s own making. In a speech at Labour’s party conference in September and in a round of ensuing media interviews, he said he wanted to begin a discussion about whether the UK should eventually rejoin the bloc, or at least move much closer by entering its single market or a customs union.

Those options all remain on the table but it’ll be some time before Burnham arrives at a preferred route, government officials said. As one put it: it would be wrong to set a direction and then rip the steering wheel off so early in the process when it remains to be seen what voters want and what the EU is prepared to negotiate. An option won’t be chosen in time for the government’s 10 year-plan, set to be laid out by Burnham in December, officials said.

See also: Asda’s flat sales end losing streak as new CEO joins UK grocer

Even though he stressed there would be no major change in Europe policy before the next election, due in 2029, Burnham’s intervention has drawn a mixed reaction from his own Labour Party, as well as from the City of London’s financial sector and other European capitals.

Many in Labour would love to unwind a Brexit decision they see as an historic mistake that’s badly damaged Britain’s global standing and dealt a heavy blow to economic growth. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, Defense Secretary Wes Streeting, Housing Secretary Angela Rayner and Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh are prominent figures backing much closer ties, government officials said.

Yet much of the party sees political risk in returning to free movement of people with the continent and aligning with its rules. Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey, Burnham’s de facto deputy Louise Haigh, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds, Health Secretary Yvette Cooper and Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy favour a more cautious approach, the officials said.

See also: Poundland files to delay UK insolvency as it finds a rescuer

All those ministers agree with Burnham that the conversation about Europe should be carefully managed and not pre-determined, views that were expressed at a Cabinet meeting on Tuesday, they said. It is better to have a responsible discussion and get it right, one official said.

However, another characterised the Cabinet divide as all the ministers who have ambitions to be prime minister versus those who want the party to win the next election.

Early feedback from the City of London and businesses has been a factor in tamping down the speculation. While British banks and executives largely backed the campaign to remain in the EU, some industries — particularly financial services and artificial intelligence (AI) — are now reluctant to realign with the bloc’s rules.

Bloomberg reported this week that the UK is opposed to rule-taking on either financial services or AI. A government official said that while they were keeping all options on the table, it would not be Burnham’s preference in any long-term negotiation with the EU to be a rule-taker in these two areas. That implies he would be reluctant to pursue a so-called Norway-style option which amounts to single market membership without being able to influence its rules.

In an intervention earlier this week, David Cameron, the former prime minister who called the 2016 referendum and campaigned unsuccessfully to remain in the EU, told Bloomberg that Britain should not rejoin.

“Instead of launching an argument about rejoining — which I think would be a very long and painful argument and who knows where it would end up — instead of that, focus on how do we be the best friend, best neighbour, best partner,” Cameron said in an interview on The Mishal Husain Show.

For now, Burnham’s priority is finalising a more modest deal at the Friday summit on trade rules for plant and animal products and youth mobility. Before then, on Monday he will deliver a speech on foreign policy in which he’ll repeat his desire for closer relations with Europe.

A government official allied to Burnham said his approach to EU policy would be conversation rather than negotiation, with the aim of fostering a better trade relationship. On the flip side of the argument, another official said it was naive, arguing that Burnham had opened Pandora’s Box without a plan for what he’s trying to achieve.

title: MAS, Bank of England and Bank of Thailand complete FX settlement trial
article:
The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), Bank of England and Bank of Thailand completed a trial showing how different payment systems could work together to make foreign exchange settlement safer and reduce the cash banks need to settle trades.

More than US$1.4 trillion ($1.8 trillion), or 10% of average daily foreign exchange settlement in April 2025, remained fully exposed to settlement risk, according to Bank for International Settlements. That is the danger that a party to a currency trade pays out money but fails to receive what it is owed.

Project Meridian FX APAC tested payment-versus-payment settlement across the three central banks’ test environments. This ensures that one currency changes hands only if the corresponding payment in the other currency also occurs.

A process known as synchronisation coordinated those payments across separate systems. Partior, a clearing and settlement infrastructure provider, developed, integrated and tested the prototype that linked the transfers.

Alongside individual trades, the project tested whether payments across multiple currency transactions could be offset against one another, reducing the amounts that participants need to pay. Combining that process with linked settlement could help banks use their cash more efficiently while reducing settlement risk.

Testing spanned conventional systems that settle payments individually in real time and systems based on distributed ledger technology. Synchronised settlement worked across systems with different technologies and capabilities, while the trial identified requirements and trade-offs involved in connecting them, the central banks say.

See also: Why the investment industry can’t sit out the anti-scam fight

Earlier Meridian FX work, led by the BIS Innovation Hub in London, provided the foundation for the project. The latest trial extended testing across a broader range of currencies, infrastructures and time zones.

Beyond the technical tests, the project examined legal, regulatory and oversight considerations. The Reserve Bank of Australia and Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas contributed as observers.

Further work could extend the approach to more jurisdictions and industry participants, as well as additional currencies and transaction scenarios. It could also examine the technical, legal, operational and governance arrangements needed to apply synchronised settlement in practice.

See also: How Bpifrance helps French fintechs expand to Southeast Asia

“Cross-border settlement increasingly takes place across systems built on different technologies and operating models. Project Meridian FX APAC has shown how synchronisation could help enable PvP settlement across these diverse environments, reducing settlement risk while supporting greater interoperability,” says Kenneth Gay, chief FinTech officer at the Monetary Authority of Singapore.

Pucktada Treeratpituk, director of Payment Systems and Financial Technology Policy Department at the Bank of Thailand, adds: “ The insights on technical integration, operating models and regulatory considerations established a practical foundation for modernising wholesale settlement infrastructure.”

“The results provide a strong foundation for further collaboration as we explore how this approach could be developed towards real-world use,” says Tom Mutton, the Bank of England’s executive director of payments, innovation and fintech.

title: Anthropic IPO set to cap year of record-breaking equity megadeals
article:
(Nov 14): Anthropic PBC is poised to add to a blockbuster year of transactions that are orders of magnitude larger than those seen in the past decade, with the biggest initial public offering (IPO) of all time joining a half dozen other jumbo equity deals.

If Anthropic’s first-time share sale prices at the top of its marketed range on Nov 18, the artificial intelligence (AI) lab’s IPO and private placement would together raise US$90.4 billion ($116.4 billion), easily surpassing the US$86.2 billion in Elon Musk’s SpaceX listing in June.

Exercising the so-called over-allotment option after the trading begins, bringing it to more than US$100 billion, would surpass Meta Platforms Inc’s roughly US$98 billion equity deal announced last month, also to fund its AI business.

More than US$425 billion has been raised across US-listed companies when accounting for IPOs, completed at-the-market share sale programmes and marketed share sales, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. That tops the 2021 total of roughly US$408 billion raised, the data showed.

Including Anthropic, the US’ three biggest-ever IPOs landed in a matter of months of each other, a sign of how deals are being turbocharged by AI companies’ need for cash on a scale never seen before. Even adjusted for inflation, this year’s biggest IPOs are far larger than previous record-holders like Saudi Aramco and Visa Inc.

While SK Hynix Inc’s US$26.5 billion US listing in July marked the largest for a company based outside of the country, its size after adjusting for inflation is actually more in line with deals from decades ago. By that measure, the South Korean company’s US first-time share sale trails debuts from Alibaba Group Holding Ltd in 2014 and SoftBank Corp in 2018.

See also: IOIPG REIT lowers IPO price to 91 sen, public tranche oversubscribed 0.59 times

The hunt for AI funding has not only broken records, it has also prompted a handful of tech giants to sell stock for the first time in decades.

Meta, led by Mark Zuckerberg, would likely hold the title for the biggest equity fundraise with its US$98 billion of offerings including a marketed stock sale and preferred shares. The bulk of the total comes in the form of a planned US$60 billion at-the-market share sale programme, which allows companies to periodically sell shares in the open market.

See also: Anthropic’s IPO is about six times oversubscribed — Bloomberg

Like IPOs, ATMs have metastasised in the AI era. Bitcoin treasury firm Strategy Inc raised US$21 billion in 2024 via an ATM and did another of the same size in 2025, data compiled by Bloomberg showed.

This year, Alphabet Inc’s roughly US$85 billion funding plan includes a US$40 billion ATM programme. Oracle Corp sold roughly US$20 billion of shares through an ATM programme, on top of raising tens of billions of dollars through the sale of additional equity and debt.

title: US stocks close lower after Nvidia spurs volatility in AI trade
article:
(Nov 14): US equities fell on Friday at the end of a volatile week as investors reassessed the artificial intelligence (AI) trade in the wake of turmoil at Nvidia Corp and the outlook of Federal Reserve (Fed) interest rates.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 dropped 1.2% Friday, while the S&P 500 Index closed lower by 0.4%. Still, both gauges managed to end the week with gains. The blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average closed up 0.1%.

Nvidia had its worst week since the April 2025 tariff sell-off, erasing over half a trillion dollars in value this week alone, to take its market capitalisation below US$4 trillion ($5.2 trillion) after chief executive officer Jensen Huang was ousted. Confidence in the world’s biggest maker of AI-powered chips was rocked by revelations of Huang’s extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy.

Concerns around the future of Nvidia’s leadership collided with investor questions regarding the cost of funding the broader AI buildout. “We’re seeing a few different factors weighing on chip and data-centre names today,” wrote Nicole Tanenbaum, partner and chief investment officer at Chequers Financial Management. “The first is clearly the uncertainty surrounding Nvidia’s leadership transition, which could have broader implications for the AI ecosystem.”

Stocks of Nvidia’s suppliers extended a sell-off and even the chipmaker’s rivals, including Broadcom Inc and Advanced Micro Devices Inc, tumbled Friday after rallying a day earlier.

Investors will come face-to-face with the possibility that more issues may come to light surrounding Huang’s departure and the suspected spy scandal, especially as Nvidia is scheduled to report third-quarter earnings after the bell Tuesday. Angelo Zino, senior vice president at CFRA Research, said that while he expects the company’s earnings to be “perfectly fine”, the bigger risk is what the market doesn’t know yet.

See also: US stocks bounce as Nvidia rout spurs gains elsewhere

“There’s a lot there that we’re probably going to discover that we don’t want to know about,” Zino said on Bloomberg Radio.

Other areas of the AI trade are attracting attention. Orders for Anthropic’s IPO are six times oversubscribed despite the recent agitation, while CoreWeave Inc recently announced plans to raise at least US$4 billion through an investment-grade loan offering.

Still, some investors are viewing this week’s volatility as part of a rotation that’s been unfolding long before Nvidia captured headlines. “This rotation has been underway for the better part of two years,” said Chris Galipeau, head market strategist for the Franklin Templeton Institute, on Bloomberg Television. “We’ll continue to see high levels of volatility,” he added, noting his belief that the rotation is “closer to the end than the beginning”.

See also: US stocks climb as Wall Street gets fresh AI fuel

In Galipeau’s view, the most accurate long-term test for AI companies will be seen in the relationship between how much each spends on infrastructure versus the return on that particular investment. “That’s where the puck is going,” Galipeau said.

Investors got some relief early Friday, after the latest inflation data eased the risk of the Fed raising interest rates by half a percentage point next month. The producer price index rose 0.3% in October over the previous month and 6.5% over the previous year, the fastest pace in four years, but slightly below expectations. That helped take some air out of December rate-hike bets, which were fuelled by hotter-than-expected consumer prices earlier this week.

“There’s no urgency to go to 50,” said Priya Misra, managing director and portfolio manager at JP Morgan Investment Management. A half-point move could lead to a “huge messaging problem” leading Wall Street to price a neutral rate that is much higher, Misra said.

Oil is holding onto its gains, with West Texas Intermediate hovering at around US$89. The International Energy Agency said on Friday that the oil market will be in surplus this quarter for the first time since the war began.
